utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher. Yes, Mr. Mundis

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: With your leave, Mr. President, I will withdraw from the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes please do so, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, I presume?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please stand up just for a while. Mr. Mole, before giving us testimony in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to make that declaration and the text will be handed out to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mole. Please be seated. You will first be examined by counsel for the Prosecution. Examined by Mr. Ierace:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, were you born on the 12th of April 1950?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I was, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1969, did you enlist in the British Army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you train at Sandhurst?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By 1992 were you a Lieutenant-Colonel in the British army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In May of 1992, were you posted to the former Yugoslavia as an UNMO, United Nations military observer?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I am sorry. I am really sorry, but again, the rhythm -- the pace is too fast. I see that the French booth is translating Lieutenant-Colonel by another expression, so we would kindly ask Mr. Ierace to slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mole and Mr. Ierace, everything that you say has to be translated into French and into B/C/S. So would you please slow down. I will try to follow the French channel so that I can keep on eye on whether they can cope with it or not. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In September of 1992, were you appointed as the Senior Military Observer for Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that sometimes shortened to SMO.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you remain in that position until approximately the 26th of December 1992?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As SMO, were you in charge of approximately 60 UNMOs in total from both sides of the confrontation lines in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, we have heard evidence in the trial so far in relation to the period that you were the SMO to the effect that UNMOs were divided into two groups. Each positioned on opposite sides of the confrontation lines and designated as Papa UNMOs for the Presidency side and Lima UNMOs for the Sarajevo Romanija Corps side. Is that your understanding of the situation at the time in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From time to time did you change the position of Papa and Lima observation posts?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Yes, that was within my remit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When doing so on the Lima side what were the priorities in determining new positions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: The overriding issue on the Lima side was to ensure that we had coverage of as many weapon sites as we could possibly manage within the manning structure that I was permitted to retain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you changed positions, or add new positions, on the Papa side, that is, new observation posts what was the priority?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: The priority on the Papa side was a slight variance from that I have already described. The heavy weapons were not so much in evidence on Papa side. So our main task was observation of the city. To achieve that observation, it was necessary that the observation posts selected had height advantage, so that would be a primary consideration. I would, however, like to add one other rider and that is that safety was of paramount importance because as we gained height for that primary objective, we naturally came closer to the front lines and lines of confrontation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that because in many instances the front line, that is the lines of confrontation were on the valley edge, that is, as one gained height from the valley floor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: That is a correct assumption.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from making --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, may I also ask you to make a small break before putting your next question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from observations made from the posts, were the UNMOs expected to move around beyond the posts in making observations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: When I inherited the appointment, there was an element of static observation posts on the Papa side. So in particular there, I was keen that we should introduce a mobility which would permit a greater coverage of the city within the limited manpower which had been allocated to me. This slight change in policy was extremely useful on the Lima side, but for slightly different reasons in that we would be able, hopefully, to monitor more weapon sites than we were when I initially assumed my appointment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they nevertheless occur on the Papa side?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How successful do you assess the Papa side observations to have been?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I take it that your question relates to their ability to observe the city, am I right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: In that case, the answer to your question is: Very successful. I would perceive that we would cover 95 per cent of the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is just to -- page 25, line 94, it is a very tiny mistake in the French translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...noticed that there was a difference. Perhaps you could repeat your answer, Mr. Mole, to the question about the successfulness, at least your assessment of the successfulness of the Papa side observations. You started your answer by saying that: "You took it that the question relates to the ability to observe the city." And then you continued your answer. Could you please repeat on from that point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would consider that the coverage of the city by the Papa observation posts was successful in that it covered 95 per cent of the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How would you gauge the success or otherwise of the observations made by the Lima UNMOs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: We had military observers on a number of weapon sites and the decision as to where they were located had been made before I arrived in the city. And, as is my understanding, as part of the airport agreement. I have already intimated that I had it within my power to change those locations, but I was bound by the agreement, and I couldn't change those locations at random. For the same reason, therefore, they didn't necessarily cover all the weapon sites which I knew existed around the city. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. It is difficult to analyse how many weapon sites around the city were not covered. So, therefore, to answer your question, on a percentage basis, to relate to that I have answered for Papa side is not so easy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as to avoid any misunderstanding, when you refer to "weapon sites around the city," which side of the confrontation lines are you referring to? The Papa side, the Lima side or both?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Within the picture that we have been discussing, on the Lima side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how were you able to determine that there were gun sites, gun batteries, that you were not observing through your UNMOs on the Lima side?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: One of the functions of the Papa side was to observe fall of shot within the city. One of the tasks of the weapon site military observers on the Lima side was to observe rounds outgoing from those weapons. At the end of each day, we would assess the two sets of figures. They were represented in the situation report that was submitted daily. The two sets of figures were mathematically at variance. The numbers of rounds fired did not always equal the number of rounds that landed within the city; the latter often being greater. By observation and deduction, there were more weapons available on the Lima side than we had monitored.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have also heard evidence that there was not direct communication between Papa side UNMOs and Lima side UNMOs. Was there communication to a headquarters from each of the two sides?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Perhaps I had better explain again the relative status of the Papa and Lima side which, if you will forgive me, I don't know whether present company understand. There was deliberately no communication between the Papa side and the Lima side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed, that was the reason that I informed you of the state of evidence so as to save some time. Could I ask you this: Did the UNMOs, when recording outgoing fire from the Lima side and incoming fire from the Papa side take note of the time of each of those events?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: One of the major forms that we used whilst making our observations, whether that be on the Papa or the Lima side, was a standardised form. It was structured to allow the maximum information to be supplied to me at my headquarters. And that form contained quite a serious amount of information. It was broken down, as I recall, into a number of serials, and each of those serials had a subletter which referred to time, place and further detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it possible with that information that was available to you from each of the two sides to marry up a record of outgoing fire and then by reference to the relative times, a record of incoming fire on the Papa side?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Yes. That was a major task for us daily. With the one rider that I have already mentioned that there would be a disparity in numbers and so clearly it wasn't an operation which ended up with 100 per cent success rate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed, was that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, could you please just take a pause. I am trying to follow the French channel. You could now continue

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed was that the mechanism which enabled you to determine that not all sources of fire from the Lima side were under observation, that is, the disparity in total numbers and more particularly the records of incoming fire which did not have a counterpart of observed outgoing fire from the Lima side?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Yes, that was the major mechanism to establish that fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, we have also heard evidence in the trial, and I say this to save time, that under your position of SMO, there was a Papa side SubSector Commander and a Lima side SubSector Commander. Who was or who were the Papa side SubSector Commanders during your tenure as SMO?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Flight Lieutenant Carl Harding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On which side?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Papa side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the Lima side?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Gwynn Rees Michael Beary. They were two that come instantly to mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Gwynn, as in Gwynn Rees, spelled G-w-y-n-n, Rees, R-e-e-s?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a lieutenant commander?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: He was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you were there on the Lima side, was one of your subordinates Pat Henneberry?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Yes. He had an appointment on the Lima side where he literally took over and looked after the Lima side for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did that appointment differ from the appointment of the Lima SubSector Commander, if at all?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: On the Lima side of their own choice, they had a substructure which was up to them to organise, but as my tour proceeded, we had more changes in term of what we called Lima 9 who was the commander of the Lima side then we did on the Papa side. That is why I name three people as opposed to the one on the Papa side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you mean by that -- do you mean by that that Pat Henneberry was a subsector commander on the Lima side?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Ye.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the Lima side subsector commander when you left on the 26th of December 1992, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I think it was Pat Henneberry, but I would have to refer to my notes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you mentioned your notes. Have you brought with you a diary?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it the case that you have not given the Office of the Prosecutor a copy of your diary?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: That is the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that because you do not wish to do so?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you are permitted to consult your diary in order to check a date or piece of information, would you be prepared to allow the Defence to look at just that part of that entry that you used to refresh your memory with the rest being covered?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. In any case, since we are directly interested in this, the Prosecution knows that we are horrified by detached exhibits without the context so we wouldn't restrict ourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are now on our way to question the witness. Let's just first proceed, Mr. Ierace, and then, of course, if such questions would arise, then, of course, you could oppose if you want to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could read that question again on the screen in front of you that I last asked, could you please answer it. It appears underneath the 100 in the left-hand column and then along side the 3, underneath the 100. In other words, that no one would get to see anything other than the specific piece of information which you used to refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: That would be fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Now, what instructions, if any, did you provide to your Lima side UNMOs as to whether their role should be passive or active and whether they should engage local commanders in dialogue?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Initially, on assuming my appointment, one of the other aspects of operation that I wished to change was to instill in the military observers an inclination to be active in their role rather than passive. One of the effective methods of achieving that was to require them to actively seek who the commanders were, what they were doing, and question them as to why they were doing it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any view as to whether the Lima subsector commander should engage the corps commander on the Lima side in direct oral communication?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: In that they were collocated, I would expect that he would do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You referred earlier to your predecessor. Who was that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Gray from the Royal New Zealand Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also earlier referred to the airport agreement. Was that an agreement which was the foundation for the role of the UNMOs in Sarajevo or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the date of that agreement? If not the exact date, then perhaps the month?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I would -- from what I recall, I think it was September 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Incidentally, do you recall the date in September that you commenced your duties as the Sarajevo SMO?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I hesitate to ask, but may I look at my diary?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If Mr. President allows you to do so. Might the witness be allowed to do that, Mr. President, on the basis that I earlier indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace -- Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, again, this is a document that we haven't seen, that we will not have a right to see except for a small piece of patchwork, depending on the Prosecution, and I don't think that we can just have a couple of notes. We would rather hear the whole piece of music.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, before going any further, could you explain to the Court the reasons why you would not give your diary, which might contain important information, to the Office of the Prosecutor? We have had several witnesses who did, as a matter of fact. I don't know what keeps you from doing it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I am sure you appreciate, a diary is a very personal record of events. Those events will be represented in sometimes emotional and sometimes nonemotional ways which opens your soul in a way you wouldn't want others to read. For that reason, I think it would be wiser if I kept it to myself. No more reason other than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can imagine that you wouldn't like to read everyone the -- from the bottom of your soul. But if that would be limited to a small number of people, I mean, we have possibilities of protecting certain information. Because I fully do understand that you say, well, it's sometimes emotional. But, of course, the Court would also perhaps be interested in the nonemotional parts that might -- since it is a long time ago, and the Court is aware that sometimes the memory was better at the time when words were written than it is perhaps some 10 years later. So it could be a source which could assist us in arriving at the truth. I am not saying it does, but it might be. Therefore, that is the other side. As you will understand, this Court is trying to come at the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand fully. But since we are talking about a date that I assumed an appointment in Sarajevo, I would suggest to you that although I don't remember the exact date, it is hardly a contentious issue to open the diary and see when I said I went to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the issue raised by the Defence is that this gives a fragmentary information on the events and not full information of what would have been in your knowledge or had been within your knowledge. But let's not at this moment argue on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might I --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Mr. President, I have completely understood what the witness means. And if it is just a date, from the side of the Defence, we agree. However, if later on we have to examine other points, then the position of the Defence would be different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you reserve the right to respond to every single issue --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am walking in the witness's steps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, not being contested any more, Mr. Ierace, in order to refresh his memory, the witness may consult his diary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I took a convoy from Pale on the 15th of September and arrived on the 16th of September, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: May I also correct something I said earlier on?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: During the question you asked the date of the airport agreement and whilst looking for the date that I arrived in Sarajevo, I noticed that in the forms which have been submitted that the date of the airport agreement was June 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you refer to "the forms which have been submitted," I think you pointed to copies of your statements; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, earlier we mentioned the Corps Commander. First of all, what was the name of the particular structure of the armed forces on the Lima side?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I referred to them as the Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the commander of that Corps during your tenure as SMO?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Colonel and later Major General Galic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a routine which included regular meetings with General Galic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I would go across to the Lima side many times during a week and would always hope to see him on one or two occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say, "go across" was your office in the PTT building on the Bosnian government side of the confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I am sorry, I assumed knowledge. Yes, I lived in the PTT building within the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed we have had evidence to that effect. Now, when you typically met with General Galic, whereabouts precisely did those meetings take place?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Within the Lukavica barracks, the Serb side had provided accommodation for our UNMO headquarters and I habitually met Colonel Galic within the same building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it in a particular room that you would typically meet him or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Often in the conference room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On those occasions that you met him, did you have the services of an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: The UNMOs on the Lima side had the services of an interpreter and it was that interpreter that we utilised for the meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who employed that interpreter and what was the interpreter's name, if you remember it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: From what I recall, she was an UN employee, but I am afraid I can't recall her name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you met with General Galic, typically, did he have his own interpreter or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: There was another individual who frequently attended those meetings. His capacity wasn't, from my perception, that of an interpreter. So the meeting relied on the interpreter that we provided.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the name of that other individual?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Captain Indjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What role did he perform from your perception by attending those meetings?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: It is an interesting question which, as of now, I haven't a direct answer to other than my personal feelings as to what he was doing. Therefore, what I say is not fact, purely my own interpretation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately on how many occasions that you met with General Galic was Captain Indjic present?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Initially, when we had our first meetings he was present quite often. In fact, one could probably say more often than not. His attendance dropped off and became more infrequent as my tour proceeded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he was present did he ever talk with General Galic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Yes. There was consultation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that in English or another language?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: It was in another language.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever address you at any of those meetings?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: He might have done. I don't remember specific occasions, but in that my intention of being there was to consult with Colonel Galic, his presence was somewhat irrelevant to me in that I would wish my conversation to be directed at the primary purpose of my visit, and that would be General Galic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On any of the occasions that you met General Galic, was he out of uniform?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Throughout the whole time I knew this individual, I never saw him in uniform at all. He would attend the meetings, as I recall, wearing a leather jacket and other civilian attire.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am sorry to interrupt the question, but there is a grammar problem. Here I am not sure what he is referring when he says "he." Is he referring to the general or to another person, Mr. Ierace? I am sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 106, line 24, on any of the occasions that you met General Galic, was "he" out of uniform? So I take it that your response was related to General Galic or am I wrong in understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are wrong, sir. The inference as I assumed was that subject of the dress was the Captain, am I right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I actually had in mind General Galic, but I understood your answer to refer to Captain Indjic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. On any of the occasions that you met General Galic, was General Galic out of uniform?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Most of the times that we met, we were both in military uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you are able to answer the next question by a yes or no, please do so. Did it strike you as odd that when you, the Senior Military Observer, met with the Corps Commander that frequently the only other person present, apart from the interpreter was an un-uniformed captain or person of similar rank?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I would like to answer the question with a yes or no, but there is precedent in our military that a senior officer will have an individual of an appointment such as adjutant in company with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Beyond that possibility, was there any other -- I withdraw that. Therefore, assuming his role was similar to that of an adjutant are you saying that would not be odd in your military experience?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: His presence would not be odd. The point of issue is why he wasn't in uniform. That I always found a little uncomfortable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that General Galic was promoted. Do you remember approximately when that was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I think, if I recall correctly, it was November 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am going to ask you some questions directly or indirectly on the issue of General Galic's degree of command and control over his subordinates. During the period that you were Senior Military Observer, do you recollect any military offensives by the Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: One in particular that I recall was the offensive in the area of Otes which was on the west side of Sarajevo during the early days of December 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Otes spelled O-t-e-s?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask the witness be provided a copy of Exhibit P3704.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please assist Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could we perhaps have two maps so that the General could follow, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, do you recognise the map in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I will do when I turn it around, sir. I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you provide this map to the OTP, meaning the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I did sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does the map show?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- before we look at the map and examine some questions, there are some questions that I would like to ask the Prosecution, but I think that we should do it alas without the presence of the witness because these are questions in relation not to the map --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...or you would rather explain that as well in the absence of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because perhaps we are going to have to raise some points that the witness is not supposed to know. I am not sure yet, but I suppose we could do it before him

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...what you intend to say, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, so if you say it has to be done now, and it has to be done in the absence of the witness, I will ask the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In order not to waste time, our intervention is in relation to the admissibility of a premarked map. So we don't know to which extent this has been done and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think I understand my learned colleague's concern and I can assure him that issue does not apply in this instance. Perhaps if he waits for the next two questions, he could then reconsider his position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I could not follow you, so I first have to read it

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you agree to wait for the next two questions if --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By the time it may be done by then, Mr. President. I don't know. That might be too late.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...the admission into evidence is still to be decided so it is never too late for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we agree on that Mr. President, but in order to avoid coming to the consequence that something is not being tendered, certain exhibits that are premarked, then it is better not to do it at all

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you just escort the witness out of the courtroom. But Mr. Mole, my I ask you to remain on standby.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My pleasure.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness will give evidence, I anticipate, that he placed the confrontation line on this map at the time that he was senior military officer. He copied the confrontation line onto this map from other maps in the PTT building, that is, the evidence I anticipate he will give. Therefore, it is not premarking in the same sense as applied to the witness Kucanin and which caused considerable concern to the Defence

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would the objection, nevertheless, stand Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly, Mr. President. But another thing, Mr. Ierace, could you tell us what were the two scales?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't hear your last few words.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What were the two scales used?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Scale of the map, yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not only this one, but the other one as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether you can tell it, but would that cause any problem as we have numerous matters --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and we know of at least a few of them, the scales, which would allow us without any difficulty to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I don't think so, Mr. President, because I am being told that this was copied from another map at the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did understand, Mr. Ierace, words that he, not put it on a copying machine and copied the lines, but that he did put the same lines on this map as he did put them before on another map; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard the same. And, however, this is a problem we would have preferred, that the map, as it existed in its origin, rather than a reproduction, a manual reproduction, but still a reproduction of a map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any other objection you would like to make at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, but we never know, Mr. President, how this was carried out. Perhaps we can find out. But it is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. a principle that we decided on, that we would not have premarked maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...we had one situation where we had to invite the witness to make new marks on a map, but let me just confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Prosecution may continue to question the witness on the basis of this map. Mr. Usher --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- may you escort the witness again into the courtroom. Although, there may not be much time left, Mr. Ierace, because we have to stop at 3.30 sharp because the courtroom will be used again at 4.00. Three minutes remaining.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, who drew the lines which appear on this map in purple?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you place those lines on this map?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: The map itself is a tourist map of Sarajevo and it was used for me when I first arrived in Sarajevo so that I could orientate myself to the events. It was also used as an operational map in operations room, but clearly this edition has no key points marked upon it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say, "an operational map in operations room" do you mean an UN operation room or some other operation room?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Within the PTT, UNPROFOR had an operations room and I had one which was directed towards my command of military observers on both sides of the confrontation line. This map was used in the latter context.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again I ask you: When did you place those lines on this map?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: These lines were placed on the map representing the confrontation lines of a date post 10th December 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do it before or after you left Sarajevo on about the 26th of December 1992?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE
utterances.text: Before I left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, I said we have to stop at 3.30 sharp. So if it would just be one question, then okay, but otherwise, we will have to interrupt. Mr. Mole, since this courtroom will be used for another case for the rest of the afternoon, we will have to adjourn now. We will adjourn until tomorrow morning at 9.00. And you are supposed not to speak with anyone about the testimony you gave in this court. "Anyone" means also members of the Office of the Prosecutor. Yes. We will adjourn until 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, my apologies. May I raise one matter very briefly and that is that I would seek to interpose Witness W at 9.00 tomorrow morning and therefore this witness to return on Wednesday at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since we will hear another witness who is available tomorrow, and not on any other day, we will -- I would like to ask you to come back Wednesday morning, same time, same courtroom. Yes. We will adjourn until tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
